one_liner: Book idiom: signed int index in a hand-written string-compare loop beats unsigned-index versions inside a std::sort benchmark.
what_it_does: Chapter02 of the book's companion repository sorts 2^14 pointers to random positions (suffixes) of one 2^18-byte, mostly-'a' string with std::sort and a comparator, compare(), compiled in its own .C file. Three versions of compare() differ only in the loop: 01 uses an unsigned int index bounded by the buffer length, 03 an unsigned int index with no bound, 04 an int index with no bound. It is a teaching example, not a library: the take-away is a six-line function bool compare(const char* s1, const char* s2) that returns s1[i] > s2[i] at the first differing byte, and the rule to avoid a 32-bit unsigned index in hot loops on 64-bit targets.
how_it_is_fast: Unsigned int arithmetic must wrap modulo 2^32, so in the unbounded loop the compiler has to keep a 32-bit index and zero-extend it into each 64-bit address; signed int overflow is undefined behaviour, so the compiler may widen the index to a 64-bit offset or walk the pointers directly (induction-variable widening). The bounded unsigned loop sits in between, presumably because i1 < l lets the compiler prove the index never wraps. This mechanism is inferred from the source; no disassembly or measurement was done for this entry. The extra per-byte instructions matter here because each comparison scans a long equal prefix (one non-'a' letter per about 1024 bytes, derived from the setup code).
when_to_use: Hot hand-written loops on a 64-bit target that index a buffer with a 32-bit counter and stop on a sentinel or mismatch rather than on a bound the compiler can see.

Comparators for suffix or substring sorting where you can guarantee every comparison ends on a mismatch long before the index reaches INT_MAX (here: distinct suffixes of one buffer with a single NUL at the end).

As a code-review rule for performance-sensitive loops: prefer int or a pointer-width index (std::ptrdiff_t, std::size_t) over unsigned int; the pointer-width types avoid the 32-bit wrap without relying on undefined overflow (not measured in the repo).
Reading compiler output: Chapter11/04a_compare1.C and 04b_compare2.C hold the unsigned and int versions alone, ready to paste into a disassembler.
when_not_to_use: As a general string comparison: compare() never stops at the NUL terminator, so two equal strings at different addresses are read past their ends. Use std::strcmp, std::memcmp or std::string_view::compare, none of which the repo benchmarks, and which may beat all three loops.
Buffers or loop counts that can reach 2^31: signed int overflow is undefined behaviour, so the int version is only valid while the index stays below INT_MAX.
When the loop already carries a bound: the gain against the bounded unsigned loop is about 1.3x in the book figures; the 2.8x is against a variant the book made slower by removing the bound.
When you need a faster sort: only the comparator changes and std::sort is untouched; the algorithmic gains are in the sibling sort libraries.

Toolchains you have not checked: the repo names no compiler version, and the direction of the effect depends on code generation (issue #2's title says 04 was slower than 03, but it gives no numbers and was closed by its reporter with a pointer to the book's undefined-behaviour chapter).

integration.dependencies: none for the sort programs (standard library only); the Chapter02 microbenchmarks (10a, 11, 12_*) need Google Benchmark
integration.min_toolchain: the idiom works in any C++ version; the build comments use --std=c++17 with $CXX 'usually GCC or CLANG' at -O3 (Chapter02/ReadMe.md)
integration.platforms: any; the effect is specific to targets where int is 32 bits and pointers are 64 bits (x86-64 and similar)
integration.thread_safety: pure function over read-only data; safe to call concurrently
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — same signature as the unbounded unsigned version (03); the bounded version (01) takes a length argument that the int version drops, so the call site changes

gotchas: The shared setup 00_substring_sort_prep.C was fixed on 2022-02-09 (commit ac595cb, 'Fixed typo in initialization of the string'): before it, memset filled only N = 2^14 bytes of the 2^18-byte buffer with 'a' and the rest stayed uninitialised, so the 'every comparison ends on a mismatch inside the buffer' property did not hold. Which version produced the book's figures is not documented.
The build comments in 03_substring_sort.C and 04_substring_sort.C both write -o 01_substring_sort, so following them literally overwrites the 01 binary and can time the wrong variant.

Each program times one std::sort with std::chrono::system_clock (one run, fixed default minstd_rand seed); the comparator returns s1 > s2, so the order is descending (harmless). Because all three variants return the same results on this data, std::sort makes identical comparisons and the printed comparison count should match across 01/03/04, a cheap sanity check.

The microbenchmarks compare a 1 MiB all-'a' scan whose only mismatch is the terminator; 12_compare_mbm_c.C (int index with an int bound) against 12_compare_mbm_d.C (unsigned index with an unsigned bound) isolates signedness with a bound, a cleaner pairing than the sort programs offer. No results are checked in for any of them.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Not an alternative to pdqsort, ska_sort or Highway vqsort: it changes only the comparator's inner loop and keeps std::sort. If a profile shows a hand-written byte comparator dominating a string or suffix sort, fix its index type (or call std::memcmp/std::strcmp) first; the sibling sorts are where the gains are for integer keys or a slow sort algorithm.
verified_claims_summary: The book, relayed by the seed lead (the repo has no numbers), reports 98 ms with the bounded unsigned compare, 210 ms with the unbounded unsigned compare and 74 ms with the unbounded int compare for std::sort of 16,384 suffix pointers into a 256 KiB mostly-'a' string, about 1.3x and 2.8x (derived from those figures). The compiler is only 'GCC or Clang' at -O3, the CPU and run count are not stated, and the setup file was corrected in 2022, so it is unknown which version of the workload produced the numbers.
